newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major takes election gamble on Europe.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major takes election gamble on Europe.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major appears to be taking a huge gamble in deciding two weeks from polling day to switch the main focus of his Conservative Party's general election campaign to relations with the European Union.

Major has spent the last six years as prime minister fighting to hold the party, which has ruled Britain for the last 18 years, together on such issues as whether Britain, an EU member since 1973, should join the EU's planned single currency and cede more sovereignty to the bloc's bureaucrats Brussels.
The gulf widened this week when two junior ministers and scores of backbench Conservative candidates published personal elections manifestos saying they would never back a single currency.
But the opinion polls putting his party almost 20 percentage points behind the Labour opposition show disaster looming unless Major can engineer a sea change in public opinion by May 1.
The boldness of the tactical switch he has chosen belies his reputation in the media as a dull, grey, politician.

For the past two days, Conservative campaign news conferences have been dominated by Major setting out his personal vision of a Europe of the nation state at odds with the centralism promoted by Germany and France.

Major scrapped an expensively produced party election broadcast due to go out on British television on Wednesday night and replaced it with a hastily recorded straight-to-camera message of his own on relations with the European Union.
But when the prime minister spoke to journalists on his plane as he travelled to Ellesmere Port in northwestern England, on Thursday for a walk-about, his rationale became more plain.
"Labour and the (minority) Liberal Democrats are keeping silent on this issue. I want it to be fully discussed," he said.

Major's central theme is that with huge decisions looming in Europe both on the single currency and on whether the veto powers of member states should be reduced, his experience is needed to steer Britain through a negotiation minefield.

Pointing to the fact that an initial meeting of EU heads of government to discuss the bloc's Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) has been called for May 18, Major effectively accused Britain's European partners of seeking to ambush a callow Labour leader Tony Blair should he become prime minister.
"They want to catch him in the warm afterglow of the election," he said.

Major is scathing about Blair's pledges to sign the EU's Social Chapter on workplace rights, to accept the end of the veto in areas such as immigrations and human rights, and to agree to the EU's Working Time directive which would limit the working week for many employees to 48 hours.
Major says the acceptance of the sort of employment rights enjoyed by people in many other EU countries would bring higher unemployment now seen in Spain, Germany and France.
With Labour having jettisoned its left-wing policies at home, Major accuses it of still being ready to bring in aspects of socialism to Britain through the Brussels back door.
"They claim these days not to wave the red flag, but they would certainly go to (the next EU summit at) Amsterdam and wave the white flag," he told a news conference.

Major candidly admitted that some ministers and candidates had been "unhelpful" on the single currency. But he did not believe this was the aspect of EU integration that ordinary voters really worried about.
"The single currency is the Westminster (London government district) chattering classes argument," he said.
Instead, Major believes many Britons have a vague fear that their country will be dragged deeper into Brussels' embrace against their will.
He believes his party can only gain from stressing that it will never surrender the British parliament's right to decide on the central issues of politics, such as taxation and spending.
